items.title: Lean Census: A Distributional Analysis of AI-Generated Lean Code
items.source_text: We compare two human-written and four AI-generated Lean libraries with Mathlib through the distributions of simple statistics of their code. We instead state security relative to a reference agent, which runs the same plan under the same runtime monitor with a model that never obeys untrusted content. The circuit-level model permits single-wire Pauli errors at every operation's qubit operands, capturing data errors, readout errors and ancilla errors that propagate into multi-qubit hook errors. items.source_text: In mainstream shared-memory languages, programmers use synchronisation mechanisms such as locks to isolate shared data accesses across threads to avoid data races. Yet synchronisation enforces only a temporal ordering, while shared memory still communicates updates between threads at every ordinary read and write. To achieve isolation, programmers therefore need to understand the connection between ordering and communication, and to apply synchronisation correctly and consistently, while compilers and hardware optimise assuming they have. items.title: Sundance: A Simple SMT Solver for Program Verification
items.source_text: We present Sundance, an SMT solver for program verification written in about 13,600 lines of Rust. Sundance combines the Cadical SAT solver with congruence closure, linear arithmetic, algebraic datatypes, and pattern-based quantifier instantiation. Sundance produces eDRAT proofs for every unsat answer. On 21,531 queries from Verus, Dafny, and F*, Sundance is comparable to existing solvers, with 26--38 times fewer lines of code than Z3 and cvc5. We further show that its components can be swapped for Z3's arithmetic solver, MiniSat, and the Semper e-graph. We have open sourced Sundance.
items.summary: Sundance is an open-source SMT solver for program verification in Rust that produces eDRAT proofs and matches Z3 and cvc5 on Verus, Dafny and F* queries.

items.title: Nonreciprocal Spherical Attention and Retrieval: Sharp Coarsening Clocks and Certified Score Correction
items.source_text: We develop nonreciprocal spherical attention as a mathematical framework for coarsening and compressed nearest-neighbor retrieval. For two shrinking acute blocks whose centers have zero skew pairing and whose total mass ratio is subexponential in inverse temperature, we prove $\lim_{β\to\infty}β^{-1}\log T_β=1-\cosφ$, without restricting particle-count growth. An explicit three-body flow has two rigorously separated metastable exponents. items.summary: Nonreciprocal spherical attention framework giving coarsening and retrieval bounds for attention dynamics.

items.title: Discrimination, Calibration, and Ranking: A Unified Matrix Framework
items.source_text: Discrimination, calibration, and ranking are the three pillars of classifier evaluation, yet no single algebraic language spans all three. A recent indicator-matrix account unifies discrimination measures (precision, recall, F1, Matthews correlation) across binary, multiclass, multilabel and related settings, using Boolean cell operations on indicator label matrices, generalised to soft labels by t-norms. items.summary: Algebraic matrix framework unifying classifier discrimination, calibration and ranking measures.

items.title: LARK: Lean-Assisted Reasoning for LLM-Generated GPU Kernels
items.source_text: Efficient GPU kernels are typically low-level and hardware-specific, and LLM agents can now generate them faster than experts can verify. Existing approaches rely on testing, which provides evidence but not a guarantee of correctness. We introduce LARK, an agentic framework that automatically and formally verifies GPU kernels against their PyTorch reference implementations. LARK proves equivalence in functional and memory behavior under exact arithmetic and establishes a new trust boundary: human effort is only needed to verify operator-level Lean semantics ahead of kernel generation time…
items.summary: LARK uses Lean to formally verify LLM-generated GPU kernels against PyTorch reference implementations under exact arithmetic.

items.title: The Scope Grammar of Natural-Language Rules: Counting and Enumerating Readings modulo Logical Equivalence
items.source_text: A rule written for people fixes its atomic conditions and connectives but leaves open how the connectives are bracketed, and each bracketing is a different logical reading that an autoformalizer must resolve or expose. We study the scope grammar, a deliberately ambiguous context-free grammar whose derivation trees are the readings of a connective skeleton and whose quotient by logical equivalence is what matters downstream. items.summary: Counts and enumerates logically distinct bracketings of natural-language rules as an autoformalization ambiguity problem.
